<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="Slowking4" />The Report of the Iraq Inquiry</noinclude>
396.  Similarly, Lord Wilson stated that, between 11 September 2001 and January 2002,
the Government’s response to international terrorism and the subsequent military action
against the Taliban in Afghanistan had been managed through 46 Ministerial meetings.<ref>Public hearing, 25 January 2011, page 11.</ref>

397.  The last meeting of DOP on Iraq before the 2003 conflict, however, took place
in March 1999.<ref>Email Cabinet Office to Secretary Iraq Inquiry, 5 July 2011, ‘FOI request for joint MOD/FCO memo on
Iraq Policy 1999’.</ref>

398.  In April 2002, the MOD clearly expected consideration of military options to be
addressed through DOP. Mr Simon Webb, the MOD Policy Director, advised Mr Hoon
that:
{{left margin|2em|
“Even these preparatory steps would properly need a Cabinet Committee decision, based on a minute from the Defence Secretary ...”<ref>Minute Webb to PS/Secretary of State, 12 April 2002, ‘Bush and the War on Terrorism’.</ref>}}

399.  Most decisions on Iraq pre‑conflict were taken either bilaterally between Mr Blair
and the relevant Secretary of State or in meetings between Mr Blair, Mr Straw and
Mr Hoon, with No.10 officials and, as appropriate, Mr John Scarlett (Chairman of the
JIC), Sir Richard Dearlove and Adm Boyce. Some of those meetings were minuted;
some were not.

400.  As the guidance for the Cabinet Secretariat makes clear, the purpose of the minute
of a meeting is to set out the conclusions reached so that those who have to take
action know precisely what to do; the second purpose is to “give the reasons why the
conclusions were reached”.<ref>Cabinet Office, June 2001, Guide to Minute Taking.</ref>

401.  Lord Turnbull, Cabinet Secretary from 2002 to 2005, described Mr Blair’s
characteristic way of working with his Cabinet colleagues as:
{{left margin|2em|
“… ‘I like to move fast. I don’t want to spend a lot of time in kind of conflict resolution, and, therefore, I will get the people who will make this thing move quickly and efficiently.’ That was his sort of characteristic style, but it has drawbacks.”<ref>Public hearing, 13 January 2010, page 28.</ref>}}

402.  Lord Turnbull subsequently told the Inquiry that the group described above was “a professional forum ... they had ... with one possible exception [Ms Clare Short, the International Development Secretary], the right people in the room. It wasn’t the kind of sofa government in the sense of the Prime Minister and his special advisers and political cronies”.<ref>Public hearing, 13 January 2010, pages 45‑46.</ref><noinclude>{{rule|12em|align=left}}{{smallrefs}} {{rh||56|}}</noinclude>
